title: Section 218 Agreements — State and Local Government Employers
expectedNextUpdate: Rarely — the Section 218 framework changes only when Congress amends the Social Security Act
notes: The PRIMARY source for why some teachers and public employees pay no Social Security tax, and it deliberately does not answer 'which states'. All 50 states hold a Section 218 Agreement; coverage is granted per RETIREMENT-SYSTEM COVERAGE GROUP (SSA's own example is "teachers in City A who are members of the Teachers Retirement System"), so it varies by district and system rather than cleanly by state. SSA directs individuals to their State Social Security Administrator. That is why this app names the commonly cited states as a prompt to check rather than as a determination — see ssa-non-covered-states-secondary.

title: States where public-school teachers are largely outside Social Security
expectedNextUpdate: Annual — both publishers refresh their coverage research each year
notes: SECONDARY, and used only because no primary equivalent exists — SSA publishes no state list (see ssa-section-218). Two independent research organisations were read and they DISAGREE on categorisation, which is itself the finding. Bellwether names 15 states with a substantial share of uncovered teachers: AK, CA, CO, CT, GA, IL, KY, LA, ME, MA, MO, NV, OH, RI, TX. Equable (https://equable.org/where-are-teachers-allowed-to-join-social-security/, retrieved the same day) splits its list differently — full exclusion vs mixed-by-district — placing CA, TX and MO in MIXED, and adding MN and UT, which Bellwether's 15 omit. Because the two conflict, the app must not present any list as a determination of an individual's coverage. Both agree roughly 40% of US K-12 teachers are outside Social Security. Revisit if SSA or a state administrator ever publishes an authoritative roster.

expectedNextUpdate: Annually, typically mid-December (2025 data expected 2026-12-10)

Bundled data pulled directly from BEA's own bulk CSV downloads (apps.bea.gov/regional/zip/SARPP.zip for the 50-state+DC table, apps.bea.gov/regional/zip/MARPP.zip for 387 Metropolitan Statistical Areas), LineCode 1 ("All items"), 2024 column — not hand-transcribed. Used only by the What-If "State Comparison" tool — not part of the tax engine. dataUrl points at BEA's downloadable state file, which is where the figures actually live; the release page named by url carries only the highest and lowest states in prose. title: Actuarial Life Table — Period Life Table, as used in the Trustees Report
publisher: SSA Office of the Chief Actuary
expectedNextUpdate: Annually, with each Trustees Report
notes: Source for reference-data/ssaPeriodLifeTable.json. CHANGE DETECTION CANNOT REACH THIS SOURCE: www.ssa.gov returns HTTP 403 to curl, including with a browser user-agent, so refdata:detect will report it unreachable rather than unchanged. That is the tool working, not a fault to route around — it is a live block on non-browser clients, confirmed 2026-08-08. The table was read in a real browser and extracted from the page's own table element rather than retyped, and the result is checked by recomputing the published life-expectancy column from the published death probabilities (ssaPeriodLifeTable.test.ts). At the annual review, open the URL by hand and compare. Note also that secure.ssa.gov POMS DOES answer automated requests — the same-day sourcing of the survivor age reduction and RIB-LIM went through it — so the block is specific to www.ssa.gov.

title: Family Maximum Chart — bend points by year of eligibility
expectedNextUpdate: Annually, with the SSA automatic determinations
notes: Source for parameters.socialSecurity.familyMaximumBend. Reachable by an automated client, unlike www.ssa.gov — see the ssa-period-life-table entry for that block. The percentages the bend points are applied to (150/272/134/175) are statutory rather than annual and live as tagged constants in engine/ssa/familyMaximum.ts; only these dollar thresholds change each year, which is why only they are here.

title: Individual Income Tax — rates and brackets
publisher: North Dakota Office of State Tax Commissioner
expectedNextUpdate: Annual — thresholds are inflation-indexed and published with filing-season materials.
notes: Read directly when North Dakota's three-bracket structure was corrected: the 0% bottom band had been modelled as an unmodelled 'personal exemption credit' with stale thresholds. Also the source for the married-filing-separately thresholds, which are genuinely distinct and NOT half of the joint ones — confirmed here rather than derived by halving. Cited as the `authority` for ND in tax-data/states/2026.json.

title: Virginia Deductions — standard deduction amounts
expectedNextUpdate: Annual — Virginia sets its own amounts by legislation rather than conforming to the federal figure.
notes: Virginia does not conform to the federal standard deduction, so its amount cannot be inferred from the IRS release the way a conformity state's can. Confirmed against the department's own published figures during the 2026-08-06 standard-deduction review. Cited as the `authority` for VA in tax-data/states/2026.json. Distinct from state-retirement-exclusion-va, which is the statute behind the age deduction.

title: US Business Cycle Expansions and Contractions
expectedNextUpdate: When the committee dates a new peak or trough — years apart, not scheduled
notes: Peak and trough months for every US contraction. The authority for every episode in historicalEpisodes.json whose dateBasis is "published": 1929, 1937, 1973, 2000/2001, 2007-2009 and 2020. Episodes whose range is a characterisation rather than a dated event (stagflation, the post-war inflation, 2022) say so in the file and cite the price record instead.

title: S&L Crisis: A Chrono-Bibliography
expectedNextUpdate: Never — a closed historical chronology
notes: The savings-and-loan episode's date range. The FDIC chronology runs through the eighties in sections; the app anchors the retiree's walk at the recession that followed, and names the longer range beside it, because what reaches a retirement plan is returns and prices rather than thrift failures. The registry URL is the one the FDIC redirects to; the /resources/publications/ path still works and lands here.

title: Updated 2026 SSI and Spousal Impoverishment Standards
publisher: CMS, Center for Medicaid and CHIP Services
expectedNextUpdate: Annually, each year in January (the January bulletin) with a revised chart in April carrying the July MMMNA
notes: Source for reference-data/medicaidStandards.json. The medicaid.gov landing page links to the bulletin and states no current figures itself, so dataUrl is the PDF; the extractor reads it through pdfjs. Two bulletins a year: the December/January one carries the January figures, the April one adds the July MMMNA and housing allowance — archive the April one.

title: Social Security Act §1924 — Treatment of income and resources for certain institutionalized spouses (42 U.S.C. §1396r-5)
expectedNextUpdate: Statutory; amended only by Congress
notes: The arithmetic behind lib/medicaidSpendDown.ts: the spousal share is half the couple's resources (c)(1); the allowance is the greatest of the state minimum and the lesser of the share and the federal maximum (f)(2); the income allowance is the MMMNA less the spouse's own income (d)(2); the MMMNA is 150% of the two-person poverty line plus an excess shelter allowance, capped (d)(3); excess shelter is shelter cost above 30% of the MMMNA (d)(4). Dollar figures in the statute are 1988 amounts indexed by (g); the current values come from the CMS bulletin, never from here.

title: Qualified State Long-Term Care Insurance Partnership — inflation protection by issue age (42 U.S.C. §1396p(b)(1)(C)(iii))
version: 42 U.S.C. §1396p(b)(1)(C)(iii), as added by the Deficit Reduction Act of 2005 §6021
expectedNextUpdate: Statutory; amended only by Congress
notes: Clause (IV): compound annual inflation protection for a purchaser who 'has not attained age 61'; 'some level of inflation protection' from 61 to 75; optional at 76 and over. States set the percentage and the original four partnership states impose stricter rules, which live in the per-state table (design §6.2), not here. The disregard itself is clause (iii): assets equal to the benefits the policy paid.

title: Long-Term Care Insurance Regulation Provisions (model law chart HS-15)
version: NAIC Model Laws, Regulations, Guidelines and Other Resources — Spring 2024
expectedNextUpdate: Each year, as NAIC reissues the model-law volume; individual state blocks carry their own review date in the chart
notes: One block per state, each with an 'Offer of Inflation Protection' row stating what that state's regulation requires an insurer to OFFER. Prose, not a table, and the state's own citation is given at the end of each row — so a curated ltcByState.inflation block quotes it rather than paraphrasing. © NAIC: cited and quoted in short, never reproduced. The chart says when each state's block was last reviewed (most read '(1/24)'), which is not the same as when the state last changed its rule. Re-pulled 2026-09-11: content.naic.org refuses this repository's fetch tool, so a maintainer saved it from a browser and it was archived through refdata:place, which gives the next review a hash to diff instead of fifty state blocks to re-read.

title: Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics — Home Health and Personal Care Aides (SOC 31-1120)
expectedNextUpdate: Annually, each year in the spring, when BLS publishes the previous May's OES estimates
notes: Public-domain wage data behind the DERIVED regional in-home care figure (design §6.3 tier 3). dataUrl is the v1 single-series GET for the NATIONAL median, which is the anchor the survey-to-wage ratio is calibrated against — if that moves, the ratio's base moved. The per-state figures come from the same API in one v2 POST and live in reference-data/homeCareWageByState.json. The wage is BLS's; the ratio from wage to agency billing rate is ours and is calibrated against the CareScout survey, so a figure derived through it is never independent of that survey and is labelled as derived wherever it is shown.

title: A Shopper's Guide to Long-Term Care Insurance
expectedNextUpdate: Every few years, when NAIC reissues the guide — the current edition is 2022
notes: The consumer guide every state insurance department points at. Two things in it back the intake rail's bands: the underwriting reality ('If you already have health problems that could lead to long-term care … you probably won't be able to buy a policy') and the affordability rule of thumb ('you may not be able to afford the policy if the premiums will be more than 7% of your income'). NAIC calls the second a RULE OF THUMB rather than a standard, and lib/ltcPrescreen.ts is careful to repeat it that way. content.naic.org refuses this repository's fetch tool, so the guide is in blockedSources.ts with the manual step.
